claim: Suicide ranks among the leading causes of death worldwide.
source: Suicide ranks among the leading causes of death worldwide (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2014

claim: In the US, suicide increased by nearly 30 percent between 2000 and 2016.
source: In the US alone, suicide increased by nearly 30 percent between 2000 and 2016 (World Health Organization, 2014; Hedegaard et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2014 and Hedegaard et al., 2018

claim: For every death by suicide, there are an estimated 25 additional suicide attempts.
source: For every death by suicide, it is estimated that there are 25 additional suicide attempts (Hedegaard et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hedegaard et al., 2018

claim: We are no better at preventing death by suicide than we were 100 years ago.
source: Moreover, epidemiological data suggest that we are no better at preventing death by suicide than we were 100 years ago (Hedegaard et al., 2018; United States Department of Commerce Bureau of the Census, 1920; Kessler et al., 2005; Nock et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to epidemiological data sources

claim: Suicide rates are rising despite the application of prevention and intervention efforts.
source: with suicide rates rising despite the application of prevention and intervention efforts (Linehan, 2008; Nock, 2016; Paris, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Linehan, 2008; Nock, 2016; Paris, 2006

claim: Theoretical models of suicide invoke the concept of 'suicidal capacity' to differentiate individuals who attempt suicide from those who only experience suicidal ideation.
source: Theoretical models of suicide have invoked the concept of 'suicidal capacity' to differentiate the small subset of individuals who attempt suicide from the much larger group of individuals who experience suicidal ideation but never resort to suicidal action (Ribeiro and Joiner, 2009; Smith and Cukrowicz, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models by Ribeiro and Joiner, 2009; Smith and Cukrowicz, 2010

claim: Most human beings are 'hard-wired' for survival and driven to avoid physical pain and threats to bodily homeostasis.
source: A basic tenet of this concept is the notion that most human beings are 'hard-wired' for survival and thus driven to avoid physical pain and threats to bodily homeostasis.
evidence: Based on established understanding of human survival instincts

claim: In individuals with heightened suicidal capacity, certain dispositional and acquired traits result in lower aversion to physical threat and higher likelihood of transitioning from suicidal ideation to action.
source: Psychological theories of suicide suggest that in an individual with heightened suicidal capacity, certain dispositional (Klonsky and May, 2015) and acquired (Van Orden et al., 2010; Van Orden et al., 2008) traits result in a lower aversion to physical threat and a higher likelihood of transitioning from suicidal ideation to action.
evidence: Supported by citations to psychological theories by Klonsky and May, 2015; Van Orden et al., 2010; Van Orden et al., 2008

claim: Non-suicidal self-injury is a behavioral factor that predicts suicide attempts.
source: Consistent with this line of thinking, non-suicidal self-injury (Klonsky and May, 2014; Franklin et al., 2011) and high levels of fearlessness of the pain involved in dying (May et al., 2012) are behavioral and clinical factors that have been reported to predict suicide attempts.
evidence: Supported by citations to Klonsky and May, 2014; Franklin et al., 2011

claim: High levels of fearlessness of the pain involved in dying predict suicide attempts.
source: Consistent with this line of thinking, non-suicidal self-injury (Klonsky and May, 2014; Franklin et al., 2011) and high levels of fearlessness of the pain involved in dying (May et al., 2012) are behavioral and clinical factors that have been reported to predict suicide attempts.
evidence: Supported by citation to May et al., 2012

claim: Interoception describes the nervous system's process of sensing, interpreting, and integrating signals originating from inside the body.
source: Interoception describes the nervous system's process of sensing, interpreting, and integrating signals originating from inside the body (Craig, 2002; Khalsa et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Craig, 2002; Khalsa et al., 2018

claim: Dysfunctions of interoception may contribute to certain mental illnesses.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that dysfunctions of interoception may contribute to certain mental illnesses (Khalsa et al., 2018; Khalsa and Lapidus, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Khalsa et al., 2018; Khalsa and Lapidus, 2016

claim: Interoceptive dysfunction is implicated in mood and anxiety disorders.
source: including mood and anxiety disorders (Paulus and Stein, 2010; Avery et al., 2014; Barrett et al., 2016; Wiebking et al., 2015; Harshaw, 2015; Domschke et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Interoceptive dysfunction is implicated in substance use disorders.
source: substance use disorders (Paulus and Stewart, 2014; Verdejo-Garcia et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Paulus and Stewart, 2014; Verdejo-Garcia et al., 2012

claim: Interoceptive dysfunction is implicated in eating disorders.
source: eating disorders (Kerr et al., 2016; Berner et al., 2018; Khalsa et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kerr et al., 2016; Berner et al., 2018; Khalsa et al., 2015

claim: Interoceptive dysfunction is implicated in nonsuicidal self-injury.
source: and nonsuicidal self-injury (Muehlenkamp, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Muehlenkamp, 2012

claim: Mood disorders, anxiety disorders, substance use disorders, eating disorders, and nonsuicidal self-injury are all associated with an elevated risk of suicide.
source: all of which are associated with an elevated risk of suicide (Nock et al., 2010; Harris and Barraclough, 1997; Smith et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nock et al., 2010; Harris and Barraclough, 1997; Smith et al., 2018a

claim: Interoception is substantially supported by the insular cortex.
source: Interoception is thought to be substantially supported by the insular cortex, with the primary representation of visceral sensations occurring in the mid-to-posterior insula, and the integration of interoceptive information with cognition, emotion, and other higher order processes occurring in more anterior regions (Barrett and Simmons, 2015; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Hassanpour et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrett and Simmons, 2015; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Hassanpour et al., 2018

claim: The primary representation of visceral sensations occurs in the mid-to-posterior insula.
source: Interoception is thought to be substantially supported by the insular cortex, with the primary representation of visceral sensations occurring in the mid-to-posterior insula, and the integration of interoceptive information with cognition, emotion, and other higher order processes occurring in more anterior regions (Barrett and Simmons, 2015; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Hassanpour et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrett and Simmons, 2015; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Hassanpour et al., 2018

claim: The integration of interoceptive information with cognition, emotion, and other higher order processes occurs in more anterior regions of the insula.
source: Interoception is thought to be substantially supported by the insular cortex, with the primary representation of visceral sensations occurring in the mid-to-posterior insula, and the integration of interoceptive information with cognition, emotion, and other higher order processes occurring in more anterior regions (Barrett and Simmons, 2015; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Hassanpour et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrett and Simmons, 2015; Critchley and Harrison, 2013; Hassanpour et al., 2018

claim: Suicide attempters and non-attempters were well-matched in terms of age, BMI, sex, diagnosis, and levels of self-reported depression, anxiety, substance use, and eating disorder symptoms.
source: We found that both participant groups were well-matched in terms of demographic and clinical characteristics, showing no significant differences in age, BMI, sex, diagnosis, or levels of self-reported depression, anxiety, substance use, or eating disorder symptoms (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis reported in Table 1

claim: A greater proportion of suicide attempters reported taking psychotropic medications compared to non-attempters.
source: We noticed that the groups showed a significant difference in their usage of psychotropic medication, with a greater proportion of the suicide attempters reporting taking such medications.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis reported in Table 1 showing 85% vs 59%, p=0.01

claim: Suicide attempters held their breath for significantly longer than non-attempters, approximately 10 seconds longer on average across both trials.
source: We found that suicide attempters held their breath for significantly longer than non-attempters, approximately 10 s longer on average across both trials (F (1, 121.84) = 4.48, p = 0.036, R2 = 0.042) (see Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (F-test) and displayed in Figure 1

claim: All participants held their breath longer during the second trial of the breath-hold challenge.
source: We also observed a repetition effect, such that all participants held their breath longer during the second trial (F(1,97.01) = 20.18, p < 0.001, R2 = 0.173), replicating previous results with this task (Willem Van der Does, 1997).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and citation to previous study

claim: Suicide attempters had higher concentrations of exhaled carbon dioxide (CO2) than non-attempters after the breath-hold trials.
source: Concordant with the increased breath-hold duration in suicide attempters, we found that suicide attempters had higher concentrations of exhaled carbon dioxide (CO2) than non-attempters after the breath-hold trials (F(1,120.33) = 5.52, p < 0.001, R2 = 0.043).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and displayed in Figure 1

claim: Suicide attempters had lower concentrations of exhaled oxygen (O2) following the breath-hold trials relative to non-attempters.
source: We also found that suicide attempters had lower concentrations of exhaled oxygen (O2) following the breath-hold trials relative to non-attempters (F(1,132.27) = 5.00, p = 0.027, R2 = 0.036).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and displayed in Figure 1

claim: Suicide attempters did not report differences in perceived breathlessness, feelings of suffocation, fear of suffocation, urge to breathe, breathing sensation intensity, unpleasantness, task difficulty, or effort expended during the breath-hold relative to non-attempters.
source: Despite the prolonged breath-hold duration and elevations in CO2, we found that suicide attempters did not report any differences in perceived breathlessness (p = 0.70), feelings of suffocation (p = 0.95), fear of suffocation (p = 0.97), urge to breathe (p = 0.76), breathing sensation intensity (p = 0.53), unpleasantness (p = 0.63), task difficulty (p = 0.48), or effort expended during the breath-hold (p = 0.27) relative to non-attempters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 ).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and displayed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The cold-pressor challenge elicited increased pain ratings over time in both groups.
source: We found that the cold-pressor challenge elicited increased pain ratings over time in both groups (F(3,276.16) = 86.78, p < 0.001, R2 = 0.589).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Suicide attempters kept their hands submerged in the cold water for significantly longer than non-attempters after reaching their peak pain level.
source: On closer examination of the LME fixed effects, we observed that suicide attempters kept their hands submerged in the cold water for significantly longer than non-attempters after reaching their peak pain level (t(278.56) = 2.78, p = 0.006, β = 0.13), without any significant differences in the amount of time taken to reach mild, moderate, and peak pain levels (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and displayed in Figure 2

claim: Suicide attempters kept their hands submerged in the icy water for approximately 18 seconds longer than the non-attempters.
source: Overall, suicide attempters kept their hands submerged in the icy water for approximately 18 s longer than the non-attempters.
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: Suicide attempters did not significantly differ from non-attempters in their retrospective ratings of overall pain, unpleasantness, difficulty, or stress experienced during the cold-pressor task.
source: Additionally, although suicide attempters provided slightly lower average ratings of unpleasantness, pain, difficulty, and stress than non-attempters, these differences were not statistically significant (unpleasantness: U = 1107, p = 0.117, FDR-p = 0.144, r = 0.16; pain: U = 1067, p = 0.122, FDR-p = 0.144, r = 0.15; difficulty: U = 1123, p = 0.090, FDR-p = 0.144, r = 0.17; stress: U = 1095, p = 0.144, FDR-p = 0.144, r = 0.15).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and displayed in Figure 2

claim: Heartbeat perception accuracy was significantly lower on no-guess and breath-hold perturbation trials relative to guessing trials.
source: By examining the fixed effects we noticed that, relative to guessing trials, accuracies on the no-guess (t(195.08) = −4.61, p < 0.001, β = −0.33) and breath-hold perturbation trials (t(195.07) = −4.013, p < 0.001, β = −0.29) were significantly lower.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Suicide attempters exhibited lower heartbeat perception accuracy than non-attempters.
source: For the second heartbeat perception model, we examined accuracy as a function of group and condition across the no-guess and breath-hold perturbation trials only (i.e. after omitting the 'guess' trial), and found a significant difference between groups (F(1,97.04) = 8.64, p = 0.004, R2 = 0.048) (Figure 3)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and displayed in Figure 3

claim: Suicide attempters exhibited lower heartbeat perception accuracy during the no-guess condition relative to non-attempters.
source: In particular, we found that suicide attempters exhibited lower heartbeat perception accuracy during the no-guess condition relative to non-attempters, t(144.46) = −2.94, p = 0.003, β = −0.29)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: The difference in heartbeat perception accuracy between attempters and non-attempters was attenuated during the perturbation trial.
source: and that the difference in accuracy between attempters and non-attempters was attenuated during the perturbation trial (t(97.73) = 2.09, p = 0.04, β = 0.14).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: There were no group differences in ratings of task confidence or difficulty across the no-guess and perturbation trials of the heartbeat perception task.
source: We did not observe group differences in ratings of task confidence or difficulty across the no-guess and perturbation trials (Confidence: U = 1153.5, p = 0.453, FDR-p = 0.67, r = 0.08; Difficulty: U = 1014.5, p = 0.766, FDR-p = 0.767, r = 0.03).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Suicide attempters displayed a tendency to rate their heartbeat sensations as less intense, although this was non-significant after correction for multiple comparisons.
source: Suicide attempters displayed a tendency to rate their heartbeat sensations as less intense (U = 1345, p = 0.028), although this was non-significant after applying a Benjamini-Hochberg correction across contrasts (FDR-p = 0.084, r = 0.22) (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and displayed in Figure 3

claim: Suicide attempters exhibited reduced BOLD activation in the right dorsal mid-insula and right posterior insula during interoceptive attention to the heartbeat versus the exteroceptive attention condition.
source: We also found that, relative to non-attempters, suicide attempters exhibited reduced BOLD activation in the right dorsal mid-insula and right posterior insula during interoceptive attention to the heartbeat versus the exteroceptive attention condition (p < 0.005, corrected at α <0.05; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis and displayed in Figure 4

claim: Suicide attempters exhibited reduced BOLD activation within the right precuneus during attention to heart sensations.
source: The whole-brain analysis revealed four additional clusters with significantly reduced BOLD activation during attention to heart sensations among suicide attempters: one cluster within the right precuneus, one within the right superior temporal gyrus, one within the right posterior cingulate cortex, and one within the right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (p < 0.0005, ACF corrected at α < 0.05; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis reported in Table 2

claim: Suicide attempters exhibited reduced BOLD activation within the right superior temporal gyrus during attention to heart sensations.
source: The whole-brain analysis revealed four additional clusters with significantly reduced BOLD activation during attention to heart sensations among suicide attempters: one cluster within the right precuneus, one within the right superior temporal gyrus, one within the right posterior cingulate cortex, and one within the right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (p < 0.0005, ACF corrected at α < 0.05; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis reported in Table 2

claim: Suicide attempters exhibited reduced BOLD activation within the right posterior cingulate cortex during attention to heart sensations.
source: The whole-brain analysis revealed four additional clusters with significantly reduced BOLD activation during attention to heart sensations among suicide attempters: one cluster within the right precuneus, one within the right superior temporal gyrus, one within the right posterior cingulate cortex, and one within the right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (p < 0.0005, ACF corrected at α < 0.05; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis reported in Table 2

claim: Suicide attempters exhibited reduced BOLD activation within the right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex during attention to heart sensations.
source: The whole-brain analysis revealed four additional clusters with significantly reduced BOLD activation during attention to heart sensations among suicide attempters: one cluster within the right precuneus, one within the right superior temporal gyrus, one within the right posterior cingulate cortex, and one within the right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (p < 0.0005, ACF corrected at α < 0.05; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by whole-brain fMRI analysis reported in Table 2

claim: The results remained largely unchanged after accounting for medication status.
source: Our results remained largely unchanged after accounting for medication status, as detailed in Appendix 2.
evidence: Supported by additional analyses reported in Appendix 2

claim: The observation of diminished interoception in suicide attempters was largely unchanged after accounting for lifetime suicidal ideation intensity.
source: Our observation of diminished interoception in suicide attempters was largely unchanged after accounting for lifetime suicidal ideation intensity, as detailed in Appendix 2 and displayed in Appendix 2—figure 1.
evidence: Supported by additional analyses reported in Appendix 2

claim: Suicide attempters show reduced responses to homeostatic threats to the body, including increased tolerance for sensations of air hunger and increased tolerance of cold pain.
source: We found that suicide attempters show reduced responses to homeostatic threats to the body, including increased tolerance for sensations of air hunger and increased tolerance of cold pain relative to non-attempters.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from breath-hold and cold-pressor challenges

claim: Suicide attempters exhibit decreased heartbeat perception accuracy.
source: Additionally, we found that suicide attempters exhibit decreased heartbeat perception accuracy and decreased mid and posterior insula activity when attending to sensations from the heart, an interoceptive organ that is vital for maintaining survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from heartbeat perception task

claim: Suicide attempters exhibit decreased mid and posterior insula activity when attending to sensations from the heart.
source: Additionally, we found that suicide attempters exhibit decreased heartbeat perception accuracy and decreased mid and posterior insula activity when attending to sensations from the heart, an interoceptive organ that is vital for maintaining survival.
evidence: Supported by fMRI data

claim: An increased capacity to engage in self-destructive and life-threatening behaviors is associated, behaviorally and neurobiologically, with a blunted sensitivity to internal bodily signals.
source: Taken together, these findings provide initial support for the hypothesis that an increased capacity to engage in self-destructive and life-threatening behaviors is associated, behaviorally and neurobiologically, with a blunted sensitivity to internal bodily signals.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental findings

claim: Prior studies have suggested a role for interoceptive deficits in suicidal behavior using self-report questionnaires.
source: Prior to the current investigation, only a few empirical studies have examined the relationship between suicidality and interoception. These studies also suggested a role for interoceptive deficits in suicidal behavior, although the measurement of interoception was restricted solely to self-report questionnaires (Forrest et al., 2015; Dodd et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2018b; Rogers et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Interoceptive dysfunction in suicide attempters extends beyond symptom measures and includes abnormalities across behavioral, physiological, and neural indices.
source: Here, using a battery of behavioral measures of interoceptive processing, we demonstrate that interoceptive dysfunction in suicide attempters extends beyond symptom measures and includes abnormalities across behavioral, physiological, and neural indices.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive experimental findings from the study

claim: Suicide attempters may be less sensitive to the physiological cascade that typically follows a homeostatic threat to bodily integrity.
source: Suicide attempters may be less sensitive to the physiological cascade that typically follows a homeostatic threat to bodily integrity, allowing them to persist at the task for longer before noticing and responding to internal physiological cues to withdraw.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the experimental findings

claim: Suicide attempters may appraise signals of homeostatic threat as less salient, resulting in slower withdrawal from aversive homeostatic perturbations.
source: Suicide attempters may also appraise signals of homeostatic threat (e.g. pain, breathlessness) as less salient, resulting in slower withdrawal from aversive homeostatic perturbations.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the experimental findings

claim: A disconnection between the physiological and affective experiences of pain may enable individuals to engage in self-injurious behaviors and to fail to withdraw from painful stimuli.
source: Based on the current findings, we speculate that a disconnection between the physiological and affective experiences of pain may enable such individuals to engage in self-injurious behaviors and to fail to withdraw from painful stimuli, possibly to the point of inflicting physical harm.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the study findings

claim: The dorsal mid-insula is sensitive to homeostatic signals.
source: Prior research suggests that the dorsal mid-insula is sensitive to homeostatic signals (Simmons et al., 2013b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Simmons et al., 2013b

claim: The dorsal mid-insula is critical to the brain's representation of visceral stimulation.
source: and critical to the brain's representation of visceral stimulation (Hassanpour et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hassanpour et al., 2018

claim: The dorsal mid-insula is critical to visceral attention.
source: visceral attention (Farb et al., 2013; Simmons et al., 2013a)
evidence: Supported by citations to Farb et al., 2013; Simmons et al., 2013a

claim: The dorsal mid-insula is critical to interoceptive memory.
source: and interoceptive memory (DeVille et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeVille et al., 2018

claim: Dysfunction in the dorsal mid-insula has been linked to somatic symptoms among individuals with depression.
source: From a clinical perspective, dysfunction in the dorsal mid-insula has been linked to somatic symptoms (Avery et al., 2014) and failure to meet energy needs (Simmons et al., 2016) among individuals with depression
evidence: Supported by citations to Avery et al., 2014 and Simmons et al., 2016

claim: Dysfunction in the dorsal mid-insula has been linked to failure to meet energy needs among individuals with depression.
source: From a clinical perspective, dysfunction in the dorsal mid-insula has been linked to somatic symptoms (Avery et al., 2014) and failure to meet energy needs (Simmons et al., 2016) among individuals with depression
evidence: Supported by citation to Simmons et al., 2016

claim: Functional abnormalities within the dorsal mid-insula may be associated with the inability to effectively attend to and use homeostatically relevant information from the body.
source: suggesting that functional abnormalities within this region may be associated with the inability to effectively attend to and use homeostatically relevant information from the body.
evidence: Inference based on cited research

claim: The posterior insula has been linked to the detection of aversive sensory stimuli and associated shifts in behavioral response strategies in mice.
source: Additionally, the posterior insula has been conclusively linked to the detection of aversive sensory stimuli and associated shifts in behavioral response strategies in mice (Gehrlach et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gehrlach et al., 2019

claim: The posterior insula is closely tied to the amygdala and threat processing.
source: and it is a brain region that is closely tied to the amygdala and threat processing (Berret et al., 2019; Livneh et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berret et al., 2019; Livneh et al., 2017

claim: Meta-analytic functional neuroimaging findings in humans have implicated the mid/posterior insula in cardiac interoception, with a particular role in attending to and accurately perceiving naturally occurring cardiac sensations.
source: Meta-analytic functional neuroimaging findings in humans have specifically implicated the mid/posterior insula in cardiac interoception, with a particular role in attending to and accurately perceiving naturally occurring cardiac sensations (Schulz, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schulz, 2016

claim: The observed blunting of insular cortex activation in suicide attempters is located within subregions that are closely relevant for aversive threat processing, conscious awareness of the heartbeat signal, and homeostatic regulation.
source: Collectively, these studies illustrate that the observed blunting of insular cortex activation in suicide attempters is precisely located within subregions that are closely relevant for aversive threat processing, conscious awareness of the heartbeat signal, and homeostatic regulation.
evidence: Inference based on cited literature and current findings

claim: A low signal-to-noise ratio of visceral input to the insula may influence interoception among individuals with certain psychiatric illnesses.
source: Prior theoretical work has suggested that a low signal-to-noise ratio of visceral input to the insula may influence interoception among individuals with certain psychiatric illnesses, who are thought to be less capable of discriminating random signal fluctuations from biologically relevant signals (Paulus and Stein, 2010; Barrett et al., 2016; Barrett and Simmons, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work

claim: Individuals with certain psychiatric illnesses tend to erroneously evaluate benign signal changes as significant, and plan and act on these signals accordingly.
source: As a result, it is thought that these individuals tend to erroneously evaluate benign signal changes as significant, and plan and act on these signals accordingly (Paulus et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paulus et al., 2019

claim: The suicide attempters' reduced mid and posterior insula activation during heartbeat interoception could reflect a 'noisier' or weaker processing of interoceptive afferents.
source: In this view, the suicide attempters' reduced mid and posterior insula activation during heartbeat interoception could reflect a 'noisier' or weaker processing of interoceptive afferents, potentially interfering with the ability to accurately detect signals from their bodies.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the findings

claim: Difficulty distinguishing signal from noise may manifest as a reduced ability to adaptively detect homeostatically-relevant signals related to pain and/or suffocation.
source: To extend this line of thought, it is also possible that difficulty distinguishing signal from noise manifests as a reduced ability to adaptively detect homeostatically-relevant signals (e.g. those related to pain and/or suffocation, as in the cold-pressor and breath-hold tasks), which could help to explain the group differences in homeostatic threat response observed in the current study.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the findings

claim: Suicide attempters exhibited reduced activation within cortical midline structures during cardiac interoceptive attention.
source: We found that suicide attempters exhibited reduced activation within cortical midline structures during cardiac interoceptive attention (i.e. dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, and precuneus) that have been previously implicated as core brain regions underlying human self-referential processing (Northoff and Bermpohl, 2004; Northoff et al., 2006; Lemogne et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by fMRI data and citations to prior research

claim: Cortical midline structures including dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, and precuneus have been implicated as core brain regions underlying human self-referential processing.
source: We found that suicide attempters exhibited reduced activation within cortical midline structures during cardiac interoceptive attention (i.e. dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, and precuneus) that have been previously implicated as core brain regions underlying human self-referential processing (Northoff and Bermpohl, 2004; Northoff et al., 2006; Lemogne et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Northoff and Bermpohl, 2004; Northoff et al., 2006; Lemogne et al., 2011

claim: The finding of reduced cortical midline activation is consistent with prior research linking abnormal self-referential processing to suicidal ideation and behavior.
source: Our finding is consistent with prior research linking abnormal self-referential processing to suicidal ideation and behavior (Marchand et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Marchand et al., 2012

claim: Prior studies have linked suicide attempts with structural and functional abnormalities within the superior temporal gyrus.
source: Prior studies have linked suicide attempts with structural and functional abnormalities within the superior temporal gyrus (Soloff et al., 2012; Pan et al., 2015; Aguilar et al., 2008; van Heeringen et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The findings provide empirical support for modern theoretical models of suicide that are built upon desire-capability frameworks.
source: Our findings provide some key empirical support for modern theoretical models of suicide that are built upon desire-capability frameworks (Klonsky et al., 2017), such as the motivational-volitional model (O'Connor and Kirtley, 2018), the interpersonal-psychological theory of suicide (Ribeiro and Joiner, 2009; Van Orden et al., 2010), and the three-step theory (Klonsky and May, 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from the study findings and citations to theoretical models

claim: For suicide attempts and/or death by suicide to occur, the suicidal individual must express the capacity to approach (rather than avoid) bodily harm.
source: One assertion shared by each of these models is that, for suicide attempts and/or death by suicide to occur, the suicidal individual must express the capacity to approach (rather than avoid) bodily harm.
evidence: Based on established theoretical models

claim: Individuals who engage in suicidal behavior demonstrate an ability to ignore—or override—the natural aversion to bodily harm that protects humans against physical injury.
source: According to these theories, individuals who engage in suicidal behavior demonstrate an ability to ignore—or override—the natural aversion to bodily harm that protects humans against physical injury.
evidence: Based on established theoretical models

claim: The observations provide early experimental evidence for the role of blunted interoception and heightened tolerance for homeostatic threat in suicidal attempts.
source: Our observations are consistent with these theories and provide early experimental evidence for the role of blunted interoception and heightened tolerance for homeostatic threat in suicidal attempts.
evidence: Based on inference from the study findings

claim: Self-reported interoceptive deficits may be greater among individuals with more recent suicide attempts.
source: We evaluated evidence for interoceptive processing focusing on individuals with a history of suicide attempts within the last 5 years, based on the report that self-reported interoceptive deficits may be greater among individuals with more recent suicide attempts (Forrest et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Forrest et al., 2015

claim: The greater psychotropic medication usage in suicide attempters might reflect an effort by clinicians to reduce further suicide attempts.
source: One possibility is that the greater psychotropic medication usage in this group might reflect an effort by clinicians to reduce further suicide attempts.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the medication usage difference

claim: Visceral pain tends to be poorly localized, often referred to somatic structures and produces strong autonomic and affective responses.
source: Examples include visceral pain, which tends to be poorly localized, often referred to somatic structures and produces strong autonomic and affective responses, as well as other somatic pain signals (e.g. thermal or mechanical pain), which tend to be discretely localized to somatic structures and produce more variable autonomic and affective responses (Sikandar and Dickenson, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sikandar and Dickenson, 2012

claim: Somatic pain signals tend to be discretely localized to somatic structures and produce more variable autonomic and affective responses.
source: Examples include visceral pain, which tends to be poorly localized, often referred to somatic structures and produces strong autonomic and affective responses, as well as other somatic pain signals (e.g. thermal or mechanical pain), which tend to be discretely localized to somatic structures and produce more variable autonomic and affective responses (Sikandar and Dickenson, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sikandar and Dickenson, 2012

claim: Cardiac interoception is difficult to assess.
source: Additionally, it is increasingly understood that cardiac interoception is rather difficult to assess (Khalsa and Lapidus, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khalsa and Lapidus, 2016

claim: Heartbeat perception tasks have been the subject of criticism.
source: Heartbeat perception tasks such as the one employed in the current study are widely used, but have been the subject of criticism (Desmedt et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Desmedt et al., 2018

source: Lastly, we should note that none of the interoceptive tasks applied in this study have demonstrated sufficient reliability to be considered appropriate for implementation in prognostic assessments of suicidality in clinical settings.

claim: Suicide attempters exhibit evidence of 'interoceptive numbing' characterized by increased tolerance for aversive respiratory and nociceptive sensations, reduced awareness of the heartbeat, and blunted activity in the dorsal mid and posterior insular cortex.
source: We find that suicide attempters exhibit evidence of 'interoceptive numbing' characterized by increased tolerance for aversive respiratory and nociceptive sensations, reduced awareness of the heartbeat, and blunted activity in the dorsal mid and posterior insular cortex, a region of the brain associated with the primary representation of visceral afferent signals.
evidence: Summary of the study's main findings

claim: The presence of specific interoceptive deficits among individuals with prior suicide attempts reveals a possible role of interoceptive dysfunction in distinguishing individuals at risk of suicide.
source: The presence of these specific interoceptive deficits among individuals with prior suicide attempts reveals a possible role of interoceptive dysfunction in distinguishing individuals at risk of suicide.
evidence: Inference based on the study findings

claim: Participants were included in the suicide attempter group if they endorsed making a suicide attempt at any point during the previous five years.
source: Participants were included in the suicide attempter group (n = 34) if they endorsed making a suicide attempt at any point during the previous five years as documented in the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (CSSRS; Posner et al., 2011) and/or life-chart interviews (Aupperle et al., 2020)
evidence: Description of participant inclusion criteria

claim: A propensity score matching algorithm was used for psychiatric reference sample identification.
source: We used a propensity score matching algorithm for psychiatric reference sample identification (MatchIt package in R De et al., 2011, 1:2 nearest neighbor method without replacement), resulting in a group of non-attempter participants who denied having ever made a suicide attempt, and who exhibited similar screening symptoms on the PHQ-9, SCOFF, DAST, and OASIS scales (Table 1).
evidence: Description of the matching methodology

claim: The interoceptive attention task engages selective attention toward naturally-occurring interoceptive sensations in order to amplify activity in brain regions underlying interoceptive processing.
source: The interoceptive attention task engages selective attention toward naturally-occurring interoceptive sensations in order to amplify activity in brain regions underlying interoceptive processing.
evidence: Description of the task design and purpose

claim: The interoceptive attention task has been demonstrated to be effective at mapping the neural basis of interoceptive attention in healthy individuals and those with depression, substance use disorders, or eating disorders.
source: We and others have previously demonstrated that this task is effective at mapping the neural basis of interoceptive attention in healthy individuals and those with, depression, substance use disorders, or eating disorders (Avery et al., 2014; Kerr et al., 2016; Simmons et al., 2013a; Avery et al., 2017; Stewart et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Blunted interoception may be implicated in suicidal behavior.
source: We conclude that blunted interoception may be implicated in suicidal behavior.
evidence: Conclusion based on the study findings
